topics.title: $_GET
topics.description: `$_GET` contains variables passed to the script via URL query parameters. For a URL like `page.php?id=5&lang=en`, `$_GET['id']` returns `5`. Query string data should always be validated and sanitized before use, as it is user-supplied input.

topics.title: $_POST
topics.description: `$_POST` holds variables submitted through an HTTP POST request, typically from HTML forms with `method="post"`. Unlike GET data, POST data is not visible in the URL. It is used for form submissions, login requests, and any operation that sends data to the server. POST data must be sanitized before use.

topics.title: $_REQUEST
topics.description: `$_REQUEST` merges the contents of `$_GET`, `$_POST`, and `$_COOKIE` into a single superglobal array. Because it combines multiple sources, it is less predictable and generally avoided in favor of using `$_GET` or `$_POST` directly. The order of precedence among sources is controlled by `php.ini`.

topics.title: $_SERVER
topics.description: `$_SERVER` is a superglobal array containing information about the server environment and the current HTTP request. Common entries include `$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']`, `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']`, `$_SERVER['SCRIPT_NAME']`, and `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']`. Its contents vary depending on the server and request context.

topics.title: Abstract classes
topics.description: Abstract classes in PHP are those which cannot be instantiated on their own. They are simply blueprints for other classes, providing a predefined structure. By declaring a class as abstract, you can define methods without having to implement them. Subsequent classes, when inheriting from an abstract class, must implement these undefined methods.

topics.title: Access Specifiers
topics.description: Access specifiers, also known as access modifiers, in PHP are keywords used in the class context which define the visibility and accessibility of properties, methods and constants. PHP supports three types of access specifiers: public, private, and protected. 'Public' specified properties or methods can be accessed from anywhere, 'private' ones can only be accessed within the class that defines them, while 'protected' ones can be accessed within the class itself and by inherited and parent classes. Here's an illustrative example:

topics.title: Anonymous Functions
topics.description: Anonymous functions (closures) are functions without a name, typically assigned to a variable or passed as a callback. They are created with the `function` keyword and can capture variables from the surrounding scope using the `use` keyword. Arrow functions (`fn`) provide a shorter syntax for simple expressions.

topics.title: Apache
topics.description: Apache is a popular web server that can efficiently host PHP applications. Apache integrates well with PHP, using its `mod_php` module, providing a stable and consistent environment for your PHP scripts to run. This compatibility creates a seamless user experience, as PHP pages are served as if they're part of the website and not just files being executed on the server.

topics.title: Arrays
topics.description: Arrays in PHP are fundamental data structures that store multiple elements in a particular key-value pair collection. PHP offers extensive support for arrays, making them convenient for storing sets of data or complex collections.

topics.title: Arrow Functions
topics.description: Arrow functions provide a more concise syntax to create anonymous functions. The feature enthusiastically borrowed from modern Javascript significantly improves PHP's functional programming credibility. The primary difference between regular PHP closures and PHP Arrow functions is the automatic capturing of variables from the parent scope.

topics.title: Associative Arrays
topics.description: Associative arrays use named string keys instead of numeric indexes. You define them with explicit key-value pairs: `['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30]`. Values are accessed by key, like `$user['name']`. They are commonly used to represent structured data like rows from a database.

topics.title: Auth Mechanisms
topics.description: When you are developing PHP application, security should always be a top priority and authentication mechanism forms it's very core. It ensures proper establishing of user identities before they can access your system's resources. PHP provides several methods to implement authentication like session-based, token-based, HTTP authentication, and more.

topics.title: Autoloading
topics.description: Autoloading automatically loads PHP class files when they are first used, without requiring manual `include` or `require` calls. PHP's `spl_autoload_register()` registers a custom autoloader function. Composer generates a PSR-4-compliant autoloader that maps namespaces to directory structures, which is the standard approach in modern PHP.

topics.title: Basic PHP Syntax
topics.description: PHP syntax is generally considered similar to C-style syntax, where code blocks are defined with curly braces, variables start with a dollar sign ($), and statements end with a semicolon (;), making it relatively easy to learn for programmers familiar with C-like languages; PHP scripts are embedded within HTML using opening tags "" to mark where PHP code should be executed within a web page.

topics.title: Caching Strategies
topics.description: Caching Strategies are integral to Performance Optimization in PHP. Caching minimizes server load and enhances application speed by temporarily storing results of expensive operations, so that they can be reused in subsequent requests. Some caching techniques used in PHP include opcode caching, object caching, database query caching or full-page caching. For example, OPcache is an opcode caching system that improves PHP performance by storing precompiled script bytecode in memory, negating the need for PHP to load and parse scripts on every request.

topics.title: Callback Functions
topics.description: A callback function in PHP is a function that is passed as an argument to another function. The receiving function can then invoke this function as needed. Callback functions are often used to define flexible or reusable code because they allow you to customize the behavior of a function without changing its structure.

topics.title: Casting Data Types
topics.description: Type casting in PHP converts a value from one type to another. You cast explicitly by placing the target type in parentheses before the value, like `(int)$value`. PHP also performs implicit type juggling in comparisons and arithmetic, which can lead to unexpected results if not accounted for.

topics.title: Classes and Objects
topics.description: PHP supports object-oriented programming, offering a multi-paradigm way of coding through classes and objects. A class is like a blueprint for creating objects that encapsulate all faculties, properties and methods. An object, on the other hand, is an instance of a class where you can interact with the class's methods and change its properties. PHP lets you define a class using the keyword 'class', set properties and methods within it, and then create an object of that class using 'new'.

topics.title: Composer
topics.description: Composer is the standard dependency manager for PHP. It reads a `composer.json` file to resolve and download packages from Packagist, records exact installed versions in `composer.lock`, and generates the autoloader. Nearly all modern PHP projects use Composer to manage third-party libraries.

topics.title: Conditionals
topics.description: Conditionals in PHP, much like in other programming languages, allow for branching in code, meaning your program can choose to execute specific parts of code based on the state of variables or expressions. The most common conditional statements in PHP are "if", "else", and "elseif".

topics.title: Configuration Files
topics.description: Configuration files are critical for PHP applications because they help manage dynamic settings like database connection information, error reporting, and many other PHP settings without hard coding, making your application flexible and secure. PHP uses an "php.ini" file to hold these settings. You can modify settings by accessing and changing values in this file. For example, to adjust the maximum file upload size, you might modify the `upload_max_filesize` directive. However, changes to the `php.ini` file take effect only after the server is restarted.

topics.title: Configuration Tuning
topics.description: PHP's behavior is controlled through `php.ini` settings covering memory limits, execution timeouts, error reporting, upload sizes, and more. Tuning these settings for production involves balancing resource usage with application needs. Runtime configuration can also be overridden per-file using `ini_set()` for non-security-sensitive settings.

topics.title: Connection Pooling
topics.description: Connection pooling reuses existing database connections instead of opening a new connection for each request. PHP itself is stateless per request, so persistent connections (`PDO::ATTR_PERSISTENT`) simulate pooling within a single process. External poolers like PgBouncer handle true connection pooling for high-traffic applications using PostgreSQL.

topics.title: Constants
topics.description: Constants are identifiers for fixed values that cannot be changed during script execution. They are defined using `define()` or the `const` keyword. Unlike variables, constants do not use a `$` prefix and are globally accessible throughout the script without needing the `global` keyword.

topics.title: Constructor / Destructor
topics.description: The constructor (`__construct`) is a special method called automatically when an object is instantiated. It initializes the object's properties. The destructor (`__destruct`) runs when the object is no longer referenced and is used to release resources like database connections or file handles.

topics.title: Cookies
topics.description: Cookies are small key-value strings stored in the user's browser and sent with every request to the matching domain. PHP sets cookies with `setcookie()` and reads them through `$_COOKIE`. Cookies can have expiration times, domain restrictions, and security flags like `Secure` and `HttpOnly` to limit exposure.

topics.title: CSRF Protection
topics.description: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks authenticated users into submitting unintended requests. The standard defense is generating a unique, unpredictable token per session, embedding it in forms, and validating it on the server when the form is submitted. PHP frameworks typically include built-in CSRF middleware.

topics.title: CSV Processing
topics.description: PHP handles CSV files using `fgetcsv()` to read rows as arrays and `fputcsv()` to write arrays as CSV lines. For reading an entire CSV into memory, `array_map('str_getcsv', file($path))` is a common shortcut. CSV is widely used for data exports and imports between systems.

topics.title: cURL
topics.description: cURL is a library for making HTTP and other protocol requests from PHP. The `curl_*` functions allow you to send GET and POST requests, set headers, handle authentication, and follow redirects. cURL is used for consuming REST APIs, fetching remote resources, and integrating with third-party services.

topics.title: Data Types
topics.description: PHP supports several data types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, arrays, objects, NULL, and resources. The language is loosely typed, so PHP will automatically convert types when needed. You can check a variable's type using functions like `gettype()` or `is_int()`.

topics.title: Database Migrations
topics.description: Database migrations are versioned scripts that define incremental changes to a database schema, such as creating tables, adding columns, or modifying indexes. They allow teams to evolve the database schema in a controlled, reproducible way. Tools like Phinx and Laravel's built-in migrator manage migration history and execution order.

topics.title: Database Transactions
topics.description: Database transactions in PHP refer to a unit of work performed within a database system, which is treated in a coordinated manner. This technique is vital when dealing with critical tasks like money transfer between accounts, where data consistency is crucial. If one part of the transaction fails, the entire transaction fails, ensuring that the database stays consistent even in an event of a failure.

topics.title: Default / Optional Params
topics.description: Default parameter values are assigned in the function signature with `=`. When a caller omits that argument, the default value is used instead. Default values must be constants or expressions, not variables. Parameters with defaults must come after required parameters in the signature.

topics.title: Dependency Injection
topics.description: Dependency injection (DI) is a design pattern where a class receives its dependencies from outside rather than creating them internally. This makes classes easier to test and reduces coupling. In PHP, DI is typically implemented by passing dependencies through the constructor. DI containers automate this wiring in larger applications.

topics.title: echo
topics.description: `echo` outputs one or more strings to the browser or command line. It is a language construct, not a function, so parentheses are optional. `echo` can accept multiple comma-separated arguments and is marginally faster than `print` because it does not return a value.

topics.title: Environment Variables
topics.description: Environment variables are key-value pairs set in the server environment and accessed in PHP via `$_ENV`, `getenv()`, or `$_SERVER`. They are the standard way to separate configuration from code, especially for secrets, database credentials, and feature flags. Libraries like Dotenv load `.env` files into the environment during local development.

topics.title: Evolution and History
topics.description: PHP, originally standing for Personal Home Page, is a popular scripting language used commonly for web development. Rasmus Lerdorf created it in 1994, and since then, it has evolved significantly from a simple set of CGI binaries written in C, to a full-featured language. PHP's journey includes several versions, with PHP 3 introducing a re-written parser and a better approach to object-oriented programming. PHP 8.0, introduced several optimizations, JIT compilation, and union types, among other improvements.

topics.title: Executing System Commands
topics.description: PHP can run shell commands using functions like `exec()`, `shell_exec()`, `system()`, and `passthru()`. Each differs in how it captures and returns output. User input must never be passed unsanitized to these functions, as it can lead to command injection. `escapeshellarg()` and `escapeshellcmd()` help sanitize arguments safely.

topics.title: File Permissions
topics.description: File permissions control who can read, write, or execute a file. PHP uses `chmod()` to set permissions programmatically and `fileperms()` to read them. On Unix-based systems, permissions follow the standard owner/group/other model. Incorrect permissions are a common cause of file operation errors in PHP applications.

topics.title: File Uploads
topics.description: PHP handles file uploads through the `$_FILES` superglobal, which contains metadata about each uploaded file including its name, type, size, temporary path, and error code. Files are moved from the temp directory to a permanent location using `move_uploaded_file()`. Upload size limits are configured in `php.ini`.

topics.title: Form Processing
topics.description: Form processing in PHP involves reading submitted input from `$_GET` or `$_POST`, validating and sanitizing the values, and then performing an action such as saving to a database or sending an email. The Post/Redirect/Get (PRG) pattern is commonly used to prevent duplicate form submissions on page reload.

topics.title: Function Declaration
topics.description: A function is declared using the `function` keyword, followed by the function name, parentheses for parameters, and a code block. Function names are case-insensitive in PHP. Functions can be defined anywhere in a file and are available throughout the script scope once declared.

topics.title: Functions
topics.description: Functions are reusable blocks of code defined with the `function` keyword. They encapsulate logic, accept parameters, and can return values. PHP includes a large standard library of built-in functions, and you can define your own. Functions in PHP support default parameters, variadic arguments, type declarations, and named arguments.

topics.title: Guzzle
topics.description: Guzzle is a PHP HTTP client that simplifies making HTTP requests in PHP. It provides a straightforward and powerful way to send HTTP requests. Guzzle can simplify your life if you often handle APIs or other HTTP requests. It's great for everything from sending simple GET requests, to uploading files with POST requests, or even handling Errors using exception handling.

topics.title: HTTP Methods
topics.description: HTTP defines methods that indicate the intended action for a request. GET retrieves data, POST submits data, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH updates part of a resource, and DELETE removes a resource. PHP primarily handles GET and POST natively through superglobals; other methods are read from `$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']` and the request body.

topics.title: if/else
topics.description: The `if/else` structure executes a block of code when a condition is true and a different block when it is false. `elseif` adds additional conditions to check in sequence. PHP also supports a shorthand `if` using the ternary operator (`? :`).

topics.title: include
topics.description: `include` inserts the contents of another PHP file into the current script. If the file is not found, PHP emits a warning but continues execution. It is appropriate when the included file is optional and the script can still function without it.

topics.title: include_once
topics.description: `include_once` works like `include` but skips inclusion if the file has already been loaded. It avoids redeclaring functions or classes when the same file is referenced multiple times across a codebase. It emits a warning rather than a fatal error if the file is not found.

topics.title: Indexed Arrays
topics.description: Indexed arrays use numeric keys starting at zero. Values are accessed by their position, like `$arr[0]`. PHP assigns numeric keys automatically when you add items without specifying a key. Functions like `sort()` and `array_reverse()` work directly on indexed arrays.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.description: Inheritance allows a class to extend another class, inheriting its properties and methods. The child class uses `extends` and can override parent methods or add new ones. PHP supports single inheritance only. The `parent::` keyword calls the parent class's method from the child class.

topics.title: Input Validation
topics.description: Input validation checks that user-supplied data conforms to expected formats and constraints before processing it. PHP's `filter_var()` function supports filters for emails, URLs, integers, floats, and IP addresses. Custom validation logic handles domain-specific rules like password strength or username format.

topics.title: Installing PHP
topics.description: Installing PHP is an essential process to start developing PHP applications. PHP can be installed on Windows, macOS, and various distributions of Linux. Places to get PHP include the official PHP website, package managers like APT for Linux and Homebrew for macOS, or bundled solutions like XAMPP or WAMP that provide PHP along with a web server and database. After successful installation, you can run a simple PHP script to verify the installation. Here's an example, `<?php echo 'Hello, World!'; ?>`, which should display "Hello, World!" when accessed in a web browser.

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.description: Interfaces define a contract of methods that implementing classes must provide. A class can implement multiple interfaces, unlike inheritance which is limited to a single parent. Interfaces contain only method signatures and constants, no implementations. They are used to define capabilities that unrelated classes can share.

topics.title: Introduction to PHP
topics.description: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a server-side scripting language designed primarily for web development. It runs on the server and generates HTML that is sent to the client's browser. PHP powers a large portion of the web, including platforms like WordPress and Facebook's early codebase.

topics.title: JSON Processing
topics.description: PHP encodes data to JSON with `json_encode()` and decodes JSON strings with `json_decode()`. `json_decode()` returns an object by default or an associative array when the second argument is `true`. JSON is the standard format for exchanging data between PHP backends and JavaScript frontends or external APIs.

topics.title: LAMP
topics.description: LAMP stands for Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PHP. It is a widely used open-source web server stack for deploying PHP applications in production. Each component handles a specific role: Linux as the OS, Apache as the web server, MySQL for the database, and PHP for server-side logic.

topics.title: Yii
topics.description: Yii is a high-performance, package-based PHP framework for developing modern applications.  It provides a full set of proven, ready-to-use features including caching, logging, a template engine, data abstraction, validation, authentication and authorization, routing, a middleware pipeline, a dependency injection container, database access via query builder and Active Record, migrations, event handling, and console tools. It's especially suitable for developing large-scale applications such as portals, content management systems, e-commerce, REST APIs, etc.

topics.title: Loops
topics.description: Loops repeat a block of code multiple times. PHP supports four loop types: `while`, `do...while`, `for`, and `foreach`. The right choice depends on whether you know the iteration count in advance and whether you're iterating over a sequence or a condition. `break` exits a loop early; `continue` skips to the next iteration.

topics.title: Magic Methods
topics.description: Magic methods are special PHP methods with double-underscore prefixes that are triggered automatically in response to specific events. Common ones include `__construct`, `__toString`, `__get`, `__set`, `__call`, and `__invoke`. They allow classes to define custom behavior for object creation, property access, method calls, and more.

topics.title: MAMP
topics.description: MAMP (Mac, Apache, MySQL, PHP) is a local server environment designed for macOS, though a Windows version also exists. It packages Apache or Nginx, MySQL, and PHP together and provides a graphical interface for managing them. MAMP Pro adds virtual hosts, dynamic DNS, and other features for professional use.

topics.title: match
topics.description: The `match` expression works like `switch` but uses strict comparison (`===`) and returns a value rather than executing statements. Each arm maps one or more conditions to an expression. Unlike `switch`, there is no fall-through, and if no arm matches, PHP throws an `UnhandledMatchError`.

topics.title: Memory Management
topics.description: PHP allocates and frees memory automatically, but developers can influence it. The `memory_limit` directive in `php.ini` caps memory per request. Unset large variables with `unset()` when no longer needed. For long-running scripts or batch jobs, careful object lifecycle management prevents memory exhaustion.

topics.title: Multi-dimensional Arrays
topics.description: Multi-dimensional arrays contain other arrays as values, creating a nested structure. They are used to represent tables, grids, or grouped data. Access follows chained bracket notation: `$matrix[0][1]`. PHP does not limit nesting depth, though deep nesting can make code harder to read.

topics.title: Database Connectivity > MySQLi
topics.description: MySQLi is a MySQL-specific database extension that offers both procedural and object-oriented APIs. Like PDO, it supports prepared statements and bound parameters. MySQLi provides access to MySQL-specific features and is faster than PDO for MySQL-only applications in some benchmarks.

topics.title: Named Arguments
topics.description: Named arguments let you pass values to a function by specifying the parameter name explicitly, like `str_pad(string: 'hello', length: 10)`. This removes the need to follow positional order and makes call sites easier to read. Named arguments can be combined with positional ones in the same call.

topics.title: Namespaces
topics.description: Namespaces organize PHP code into logical groups and prevent naming conflicts between classes, functions, and constants in different libraries. They are declared with the `namespace` keyword at the top of a file. The backslash (`\`) is the namespace separator. Namespaces are essential in modern PHP applications using Composer-managed packages.

topics.title: Nginx
topics.description: Nginx is a high-performance web server and reverse proxy commonly used to serve PHP applications via PHP-FPM using the FastCGI protocol. It handles static file serving efficiently and is configured through declarative block-based config files. Nginx is the preferred web server for high-concurrency PHP deployments.

topics.title: Null Coalescing Operator
topics.description: The Null Coalescing Operator (??) in PHP is a simple and useful tool for handling variables that might not be set. It allows developers to provide a default value when the variable happens not to have a value. It is similar to the ternary operator, but instead of checking whether a variable is true or false, it checks if it is set or null. This makes it a handy tool for handling optional function arguments or form inputs. Here's an example: `$username = $_POST['username'] ?? 'Guest';`. In this line, if 'username' was set in the POST array, $username will be set to that value. If not, it will be set to 'Guest'.

topics.title: Null Safe Operator
topics.description: The Null Safe Operator is a handy feature in PHP which deals with an issue that often pops up when working with objects: trying to access properties or methods on an object that might be null. Instead of a fatal error, the PHP Null Safe Operator (indicated by ?->) allows null values to be returned safely, making your code more robust. Here's a quick example, consider $session?->user?->name. If $session or user is null, PHP will stop further execution and simply return null. This makes PHP more resilient when processing unpredictable data.

topics.title: Object-Relational Mapping (ORM)
topics.description: An ORM maps database tables to PHP classes and rows to objects, allowing you to interact with the database using object-oriented code instead of raw SQL. Doctrine is the most widely used PHP ORM; Laravel's Eloquent is another popular option. ORMs handle query building, relationships, and schema mapping automatically.
resources: What is an Object Relational Mapping (ORM)

topics.title: OOP Fundamentals
topics.description: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in PHP organizes code around classes and objects. A class defines properties and methods; an object is an instance of a class. OOP enables encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism, making large codebases easier to organize and maintain.

topics.title: Opcode Caching
topics.description: Opcode caching stores the compiled bytecode of PHP scripts in memory so subsequent requests skip the parsing and compilation step. OPcache is the built-in PHP opcode cache and is enabled by default in modern PHP. It significantly reduces CPU usage and response time for applications serving repeated requests.

topics.title: Packagist
topics.description: Packagist is the primary package repository for PHP, providing a service for hosting and distributing PHP package dependencies. Developers can use it to upload their PHP packages and share them with other developers globally. In conjunction with Composer, Packagist helps manage package versions and resolve dependencies for PHP, acting as a crucial part of modern PHP development.

topics.title: Parameters / Return Values
topics.description: Parameters are variables listed in the function signature that receive values when the function is called. PHP passes arguments by value by default, meaning changes inside the function don't affect the original variable. Prefixing a parameter with `&` passes it by reference. The `return` statement sends a value back to the caller.

topics.title: Password Hashing
topics.description: PHP provides `password_hash()` to securely hash passwords using bcrypt or Argon2. The resulting hash includes the algorithm, cost factor, and salt, so no separate salt storage is needed. `password_verify()` checks a plaintext password against a stored hash. Using MD5 or SHA1 for passwords is insecure and should be avoided.

topics.title: Database Connectivity > PDO
topics.description: PDO (PHP Data Objects) is a database abstraction layer that provides a consistent interface for connecting to multiple database types, including MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite. It supports prepared statements, which protect against SQL injection. PDO uses a DSN string to specify the driver and connection parameters.

topics.title: Performance Optimization
topics.description: PHP performance optimization focuses on reducing response time and server load. Common approaches include using opcode caching with OPcache, reducing database queries, leveraging HTTP caching, profiling with Xdebug or Blackfire, and writing efficient loops and data structures. Application-level caching with Redis or Memcached can significantly reduce repeated computation.

topics.title: Pest
topics.description: Pest is a modern PHP testing framework built on top of PHPUnit. It offers a more expressive, function-based syntax that reduces boilerplate and improves readability. Pest supports all PHPUnit features while adding its own: higher-order tests, parallel execution, and architecture testing. It is popular in Laravel communities.

topics.title: Phan
PHP CS Fixer
topics.description: PHP CS Fixer automatically reformats PHP code to comply with coding standards. It supports PSR standards and allows custom rule configurations. Unlike PHP_CodeSniffer, its primary mode is fixing rather than reporting. It is configured via a `.php-cs-fixer.php` file and integrates with editor plugins and CI workflows.

topics.title: PHP-FIG
topics.description: PHP-FIG, also known as the PHP Framework Interoperability Group, is a vital part of PHP's ecosystem. This group has the main goal of creating PHP standards that promote interoperability among PHP frameworks, libraries, and other pieces of PHP based software. The group is responsible for PSR standards, which most modern PHP codes adhere to. Typically, it provides guidelines on coding style, logger interface, http cache, and more. Each PSR is designed to make PHP code more consistent and maintainable. By adhering to PHP-FIG's standards, developers enhance their ability to integrate and leverage third-party code within their projects.

topics.title: PHP-FPM
topics.description: PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager) is an alternative PHP FastCGI implementation designed for high-traffic sites. It manages a pool of worker processes that handle incoming requests, supports dynamic and static process scaling, and can be configured with per-pool settings. PHP-FPM pairs with Nginx or Apache using the FastCGI protocol.

topics.title: PHP Versions and Features
topics.description: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) versions are critically important as each release comes with new features, improvements, and bug fixes. PHP versions start from PHP 1.0 released in 1995 and have improved over the years. The more recent version as of writing is PHP 8.0, which introduced features like the JIT compiler, named arguments, match expressions, and more. Remember, sticking to officially supported versions, like PHP 7.4 or 8.0, ensures security updates and performance improvements. For instance, the code `echo "Current PHP version: " . phpversion();` would tell you the PHP version in use.

topics.title: PHP CodeSniffer
topics.description: PHP CodeSniffer is a tool used to ensure your PHP code adheres to a defined coding standard. It works by tokenizing your code and detecting violations of a pre-configured set of rules, covering aspects like indentation, spacing, naming conventions, and more. This helps maintain code consistency across projects and teams, making it easier to read, understand, and maintain.

topics.title: PHPStan
topics.description: PHPStan is a static analysis tool for PHP that finds bugs by analyzing types and logic without running the code. It operates on configurable strictness levels (0–9), with higher levels catching more issues. PHPStan understands PHPDoc annotations and can be extended with custom rules for framework-specific patterns.

topics.title: PHPUnit
topics.description: PHPUnit is the de facto testing framework for PHP. It supports unit tests, integration tests, and test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes). Test classes extend `PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase` and use assertion methods like `assertEquals()` and `assertNull()`. PHPUnit integrates with CI pipelines and code coverage tools.

topics.title: Polymorphism
topics.description: Polymorphism allows different classes to be used through a common interface while each provides its own implementation. In PHP, this is achieved through method overriding and interface implementation. Code that depends on an interface or abstract type can work with any concrete class that satisfies it.

topics.title: print
topics.description: The 'print' statement in PHP is an in-built function used for outputting one or more strings. Unlike 'echo', it is not a language construct and has a return value. However, it is slower because it uses expressions. The text or numeric data that 'print' outputs can be shown directly or stored in a variable. For instance, to print a string you may use `print("Hello, World!");`, and for using it with a variable, `echo $variable;` is suitable.

topics.title: print_r
topics.description: The print\_r function in PHP is used to print human-readable information about a variable, ranging from simple values to more complex, multi-dimensional arrays and objects. It's exceptionally helpful while debugging, providing more information about the variable's contents than the echo or print functions. For example, in the code `$array = array('apple', 'banana', 'cherry'); print_r($array);`, it will display Array ( \[0\] => apple \[1\] => banana \[2\] => cherry ).

topics.title: Process Control
topics.description: PHP can manage processes using the PCNTL extension, which provides functions for forking, signaling, and waiting on child processes. Process control is used in CLI scripts and long-running daemons. Signal handling with `pcntl_signal()` allows graceful shutdown or custom responses to OS signals like SIGTERM.

topics.title: Profiling Techniques
topics.description: Profiling identifies which parts of a PHP application consume the most time or memory. Xdebug's profiler generates cachegrind files visualized with tools like KCachegrind. Blackfire.io provides detailed call graphs and timeline views without the overhead of Xdebug in production. Tideways is another option for continuous profiling.

topics.title: Properties and Methods
topics.description: Properties are variables defined within a class that hold an object's state. Methods are functions defined within a class that define its behavior. Both can be `public`, `protected`, or `private`, controlling their visibility. PHP 8 introduced promoted constructor properties to reduce boilerplate.

topics.title: Psalm
topics.description: Psalm is a static analysis tool developed by Vimeo that focuses on type safety in PHP. It uses PHPDoc annotations and native type hints to infer and check types across the codebase. Psalm supports a security analysis mode that tracks tainted user input through the code to detect potential vulnerabilities.

topics.title: PSR Standards
topics.description: PSR (PHP Standard Recommendations) are specifications published by PHP-FIG that define common interfaces and conventions for PHP projects. Key PSRs include PSR-4 (autoloading), PSR-7 (HTTP message interfaces), PSR-12 (coding style), and PSR-3 (logging interface). Adhering to PSR standards makes libraries easier to integrate and swap.

topics.title: Reading Files
topics.description: PHP reads file contents using functions like `file_get_contents()` for reading the entire file as a string, and `fopen()` with `fread()` for reading in chunks. `file()` reads a file into an array of lines. File reading is used for logs, configuration files, uploads, and data imports.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.description: Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Each recursive call must move toward a base case that stops the recursion. PHP supports recursion but does not optimize tail calls, so deep recursion can exhaust the call stack.

topics.title: require
topics.description: `require` includes and evaluates a specified PHP file. If the file is not found, PHP throws a fatal error and halts execution. It is used when the included file is mandatory for the script to run, such as a configuration file or a class definition.

topics.title: require_once
topics.description: `require_once` works like `require` but checks whether the file has already been included and skips it if so. This prevents duplicate declarations of classes, functions, or constants when the same file might be included from multiple places. It is commonly used in class autoloading and bootstrap files.

topics.title: Sanitization Techniques
topics.description: Sanitization removes or encodes unsafe characters from user input before using it in output, queries, or commands. PHP provides `htmlspecialchars()` to escape HTML, `strip_tags()` to remove HTML tags, and `filter_var()` with filters like `FILTER_SANITIZE_EMAIL`. Sanitization reduces the risk of XSS and injection attacks.

topics.title: Sessions
topics.description: Sessions store user data on the server across multiple requests. A session is started with `session_start()`, and data is stored in the `$_SESSION` superglobal. PHP sends the session ID to the client as a cookie by default. Sessions expire when the browser closes or after a configurable timeout.

topics.title: SQL Injection
topics.description: SQL injection occurs when unvalidated user input is interpolated directly into a SQL query, allowing attackers to manipulate the query. The fix is to use prepared statements with parameterized queries through PDO or MySQLi. Never construct SQL strings by concatenating user input directly.

topics.title: State Management
topics.description: HTTP is stateless, so PHP uses sessions and cookies to maintain state between requests. Sessions store data on the server and identify the user with a session ID sent in a cookie. Cookies store small pieces of data directly in the browser. Together they enable features like login persistence, shopping carts, and user preferences.

topics.title: Static Analysis
topics.description: Static analysis examines PHP code for errors, type inconsistencies, and potential bugs without executing it. Tools analyze the codebase and report issues like undefined variables, incorrect method calls, or type mismatches. Static analysis catches bugs early in development and improves code quality over time.

topics.title: Static Methods and Properties
topics.description: Static members belong to the class itself rather than to any instance. They are declared with the `static` keyword and accessed using `ClassName::method()` or `self::`. Static properties retain their value across all instances. Static methods are commonly used for utility functions and factory patterns.

topics.title: Style Tools
topics.description: Style Tools in PHP are primarily coding standard tools that help maintain a consistent coding style throughout your PHP project. PHP\_CodeSniffer is a popular tool in this category. It tokenizes PHP, JavaScript, and CSS files and detects violations of a defined set of coding standards. A brief example of PHP\_CodeSniffer usage would be to run it in the command line like this: `phpcs /path/to/code/myfile.php`. Other tools, such as PHP CS Fixer, can automatically correct coding standard violations.

topics.title: switch
topics.description: The `switch` statement compares a single expression against multiple possible values using `case` labels. PHP uses loose comparison (`==`) in switch cases. Each case should end with `break` to prevent fall-through into the next case. `default` handles any value not matched by a case.

topics.title: Symfony
topics.description: Symfony is a mature PHP framework and a collection of reusable components. It follows MVC conventions and emphasizes flexibility through dependency injection, event dispatchers, and a powerful routing and templating system (Twig). Many other PHP projects and frameworks, including Drupal and API Platform, are built on Symfony components.

topics.title: Traits
topics.description: Traits are a mechanism for code reuse in single-inheritance languages like PHP. A trait defines methods that can be inserted into any class using the `use` keyword. A class can use multiple traits simultaneously. Traits are useful for sharing behavior across classes that don't share a common parent.

topics.title: Type Declarations
topics.description: Type declarations specify the expected types for function parameters, return values, and class properties. PHP supports scalar types (`int`, `string`, `bool`, `float`), compound types (`array`, `callable`), class types, nullable types (`?Type`), union types (`Type1|Type2`), and the `mixed` type. Strict mode enforces types without implicit coercion.

topics.title: var_dump
topics.description: `var_dump()` outputs the type and value of one or more variables. For arrays and objects, it recursively displays the structure and types of all nested values. It is primarily used during debugging to inspect what a variable actually contains.

topics.title: Variables and Scope
topics.description: Variables in PHP are declared with a `$` prefix and hold values of any type. Scope determines where a variable is accessible: variables defined outside a function are global and not accessible inside functions unless declared with the `global` keyword. PHP also supports static variables, which retain their value between function calls.

topics.title: Variadic Functions
topics.description: Variadic functions accept a variable number of arguments using the `...` spread operator in the parameter list, like `function sum(...$numbers)`. All extra arguments are collected into an array. The spread operator can also be used in function calls to unpack an array into arguments.

topics.title: WAMP
topics.description: WAMP is a popular software stack used for developing PHP web applications on Windows systems. Acting as an abbreviation for Windows, Apache, MySQL, and PHP, WAMP provides all the components necessary to set up a local web server. Apache is used to handle HTTP requests, MySQL manages the databases, and PHP serves as the programming language. The benefit of using WAMP lies in its convenience as it pre-packages all these components, saving time for the developer. You can download WAMP from its official website, then after installation, testing of your PHP scripts can be done locally without needing an internet connection.

topics.title: What is PHP?
topics.description: PHP, an acronym for Hypertext Preprocessor, is a popular server-side scripting language favored for web development. It's versatile, dynamic, and can be embedded seamlessly into HTML code. PHP scripts are executed on the server, and the result is sent back to the browser as plain HTML.

topics.title: Writing Files
topics.description: PHP writes to files using `file_put_contents()` for simple writes or `fopen()` with `fwrite()` for more control. The `FILE_APPEND` flag appends to an existing file instead of overwriting it. File locking with `LOCK_EX` prevents race conditions when multiple processes write concurrently.

topics.title: XAMPP
topics.description: XAMP (Cross-Platform, Apache, MariaDB, PHP) is a lightweight local development stack. It bundles Apache, MariaDB, and PHP into a single installer, making it easy to run a web server locally without manual configuration. It is commonly used on Linux and less widely distributed than XAMPP.

topics.title: Xdebug
topics.description: Xdebug is the most widely used PHP debugging and profiling extension. It supports step debugging via the DAP protocol, integrating with editors like VS Code and PhpStorm. Xdebug also provides stack traces, code coverage analysis for use with PHPUnit, and profiling output in cachegrind format.

topics.title: XML Processing
topics.description: PHP processes XML using two main approaches: SimpleXML for straightforward access to XML data as objects, and the DOM extension for full programmatic control over the document tree. `XMLReader` handles large XML files efficiently by streaming rather than loading the entire document into memory.

topics.title: XSS Prevention
topics.description: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when untrusted data is rendered in the browser as executable script. The primary defense in PHP is escaping output with `htmlspecialchars()` when rendering user-supplied content in HTML. Content Security Policy headers provide an additional layer of protection at the browser level.

topics.title: Yii
topics.description: Yii is a high-performance PHP framework suited for developing large-scale web applications. It uses a component-based architecture and includes built-in support for caching, authentication, RBAC, and database access via its Active Record implementation. Yii 2 is the stable release; Yii 3 is a more modular redesign.

topics.title: Zend Debugger
topics.description: Zend Debugger is a PHP extension that enables remote debugging of PHP applications, typically within Zend-based development environments. It allows step-by-step execution, variable inspection, and breakpoints. It is less commonly used today compared to Xdebug but is found in enterprise setups using Zend Server.
